title: Swift Plunder and Who to Fear
overview: As enemy kings threaten Judah, Isaiah warns that mighty Assyria will sweep through the region, and he calls people to trust God rather than give in to panic or turn to the dead for answers.

parts.label: A child named as a warning (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Isaiah writes a strange name in public before two trusted witnesses, then gives it to his newborn son: it means roughly "quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil." Within a year or two, before the baby could say "Daddy," Assyria would loot Damascus (capital of Syria) and Samaria (capital of northern Israel), the two kingdoms then threatening Judah.

parts.label: Gentle stream, raging river (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: Shiloah was a quiet water channel in Jerusalem, standing for God's steady care, while the Euphrates in flood stands for Assyria's huge army. Because the people turned from that quiet trust, the flood would also pour into Judah up to the neck, near drowning but not over the head, in the land called by the name Immanuel, "God with us."

parts.label: Nations' plans will fail (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Isaiah dares the hostile nations to rage and plot, saying their plans will collapse. His reason is the meaning of Immanuel itself: God is with us.

parts.label: Fear God, not rumors (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: God tells Isaiah not to share the public panic about plots and alliances, but to treat the LORD alone as holy and worthy of awe. To those who trust, God is a safe refuge, but to those who don't, he becomes a stone they trip over, an image Christians later read as pointing to Jesus.

parts.label: Sealing the message and waiting (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Isaiah has his message wrapped up and kept safe among his followers, so it can be checked when events unfold. Though God seems hidden, Isaiah chooses to wait, and he says he and his children, with their meaningful names, are living signs to the nation.

parts.label: Asking the dead, finding darkness (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: In the crisis some urged people to consult mediums who claimed to speak with the dead, a practice Israel's law forbade, but Isaiah asks why the living would ask the dead instead of their God. Those who reject God's teaching will wander hungry and angry, cursing their king and God, surrounded by deep gloom.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether "Immanuel" here refers only to a child in Isaiah's own day, only to Jesus, or to both at once.
think: When the news is full of threats, what shapes which dangers you let yourself fear most?
